pos: n. (proper name; firstborn of Asher; also a Levite)
etymology: Hebrew Yimnah, prosperity or he assigns, from manah, to number, to allot; the same name as Jimnah and Jimna.
biblical_def: Imnah is the firstborn of Asher, and the name of a Levite in Hezekiah's day. “The sons of Asher; Imnah, and Isuah, and Ishuai, and Beriah, and Serah their sister” (1 Chronicles 7:30). Genesis spells him Jimnah: “And the sons of Asher; Jimnah, and Ishuah, and Isui, and Beriah, and Serah their sister” (Genesis 46:17); Numbers gives the clan, “of Jimna, the family of the Jimnites” (Numbers 26:44). One man stands behind all three spellings. He went down into Egypt with Jacob and became the head of a family in Israel. The second Imnah was a Levite whose son served in Hezekiah's reformation: “And Kore the son of Imnah the Levite, the porter toward the east, was over the freewill offerings of God, to distribute the oblations of the LORD, and the most holy things” (2 Chronicles 31:14). The first Imnah founded a family; the second raised a son trusted with the holy things. The name means he numbers, and God numbered both.

pos: n. (proper name; third son of Naphtali)
etymology: Hebrew Yetser, form, frame, purpose, from yatsar, to form, to fashion as a potter.
biblical_def: Jezer is the third son of Naphtali and head of the family of the Jezerites. “And the sons of Naphtali; Jahzeel, and Guni, and Jezer, and Shillem” (Genesis 46:24). In the census on the plains of Moab: “Of Jezer, the family of the Jezerites: of Shillem, the family of the Shillemites” (Numbers 26:49). Chronicles names the brothers “the sons of Bilhah” (1 Chronicles 7:13). Jezer's name is the Hebrew word for frame or form, used of the potter's work and of man himself: God “knoweth our frame” (Psalm 103:14), and the same word names the imagination of the heart. Naphtali's blessing was, “Naphtali is a hind let loose: he giveth goodly words” (Genesis 49:21). Jezer went down to Egypt among the seventy souls of Jacob's house and came out a family. His name is a quiet confession that God is the Potter who forms both men and nations.

etymology: Hebrew Yachtse'el, God divides or God allots, from chatsah, to divide; spelled Jahziel in 1 Chronicles 7:13.
biblical_def: Jahzeel is the firstborn of Naphtali. “And the sons of Naphtali; Jahzeel, and Guni, and Jezer, and Shillem” (Genesis 46:24). He headed the first family of the tribe: “Of the sons of Naphtali after their families: of Jahzeel, the family of the Jahzeelites: of Guni, the family of the Gunites” (Numbers 26:48). Chronicles spells him Jahziel (1 Chronicles 7:13). His name means God divides, and it is fitting for the head of a tribe whose portion God divided by lot in the north of Canaan, around the Sea of Galilee. Moses blessed that portion: “O Naphtali, satisfied with favour, and full with the blessing of the LORD: possess thou the west and the south” (Deuteronomy 33:23). Centuries later Isaiah promised that the land of Naphtali, first to be darkened by Assyria, would see a great light, and Christ fulfilled it when He made His home at Capernaum. The firstborn of Naphtali stands at the head of a tribe whose land became the stage of the Messiah's ministry.

pos: n. (proper name; son of Issachar; also a man of Ezra's day)
etymology: Hebrew Yashub, he returns or he will return, from shub, to turn back, to return.
biblical_def: Jashub is the third son of Issachar, and the name of a man who put away a foreign wife in Ezra's day. Genesis gives the son of Issachar as Job: “And the sons of Issachar; Tola, and Phuvah, and Job, and Shimron” (Genesis 46:13), with the margin noting the form Jashub. The census reads, “Of Jashub, the family of the Jashubites: of Shimron, the family of the Shimronites” (Numbers 26:24), and Chronicles agrees: “Now the sons of Issachar were, Tola, and Puah, Jashub, and Shimron, four” (1 Chronicles 7:1). He is not to be confused with the patriarch Job. The later Jashub was of the sons of Bani, among those who had taken strange wives (Ezra 10:29), and who, at Ezra's call, separated themselves in repentance. The name means he returns, the root of the great Old Testament word for repentance. Isaiah named his son Shearjashub, a remnant shall return. In Ezra's Jashub the name became a deed.

pos: n. (proper name; an Asherite, son of Helem)
etymology: Hebrew Yimna', he restrains or God keeps back, from mana', to withhold.
biblical_def: Imna is an Asherite, the son of Helem, named in the last section of Asher's genealogy. “And the sons of his brother Helem; Zophah, and Imna, and Shelesh, and Amal” (1 Chronicles 7:35). He is distinct from Imnah the firstborn of Asher; the Hebrew names differ in their roots. Asher's blessing was richness: “Out of Asher his bread shall be fat, and he shall yield royal dainties” (Genesis 49:20). Moses added, “Let Asher be blessed with children; let him be acceptable to his brethren, and let him dip his foot in oil” (Deuteronomy 33:24). The blessing of children was fulfilled in the long registers of 1 Chronicles 7, which close with the summary, “All these were the children of Asher, heads of their father's house, choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes” (1 Chronicles 7:40). Imna is one of those heads. His name may mean he restrains, a name that confesses God's hand over what is given and what is withheld.

pos: n. (proper name; an Asherite, son of Zophah)
etymology: Hebrew Yimrah, he resists or stubborn, from marah, to be rebellious; the sense is uncertain.
biblical_def: Imrah is an Asherite, the son of Zophah. “The sons of Zophah; Suah, and Harnepher, and Shual, and Beri, and Imrah” (1 Chronicles 7:36). He belongs to the house of Helem in the genealogy of Asher (1 Chronicles 7:35), which the Chronicler sums up as “choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes” (1 Chronicles 7:40). His name may come from a root meaning to resist or rebel, a strange name among choice men; parents in Israel sometimes named children for circumstances of birth, as Rachel named Benoni. Whatever the sense, Imrah's name stands in the book because he stood in the covenant people. Asher's tribe dwelt on the coast and was slow to drive out the Canaanites, but at the end of the Old Testament an Asherite woman, Anna, greeted the infant Christ in the temple. The faithful remnant of the tribe was never lost.

pos: n. (proper name; an Asherite, son of Helem)
etymology: Hebrew Tsophach, bellied jug or spreading; the sense is uncertain.
biblical_def: Zophah is an Asherite, the eldest named son of Helem and the father of a large house. “And the sons of his brother Helem; Zophah, and Imna, and Shelesh, and Amal” (1 Chronicles 7:35). “The sons of Zophah; Suah, and Harnepher, and Shual, and Beri, and Imrah” (1 Chronicles 7:36), and the list continues with six more in the next verse, eleven sons in all. In Zophah's house the blessing Moses spoke over the tribe was fulfilled: “Let Asher be blessed with children; let him be acceptable to his brethren, and let him dip his foot in oil” (Deuteronomy 33:24). Children are the heritage of the LORD, and Zophah's quiver was full. The Chronicler's summary, “All these were the children of Asher, heads of their father's house” (1 Chronicles 7:40), places him among the princes of a tribe that numbered twenty-six thousand fit for war. A man known only as the father of eleven sons is remembered as a man God blessed.

pos: n. (proper name; a Horite of Seir; also an Asherite)
etymology: Hebrew Yithran, excellent, abundance, from yathar, to remain over, to excel.
biblical_def: Ithran is the name of a Horite chief's son in Seir and of an Asherite. The first is in the genealogy of the Horites who held Seir before Esau: “These are the sons of Seir the Horite, who inhabited the land; Lotan, and Shobal, and Zibeon, and Anah” (Genesis 36:20). “And these are the children of Dishon; Hemdan, and Eshban, and Ithran, and Cheran” (Genesis 36:26), repeated in 1 Chronicles 1:41. The Horites were displaced by Esau's sons, as Israel would displace the Canaanites; God gave Mount Seir to Esau for a possession. The second Ithran is an Asherite in the house of Zophah: “Bezer, and Hod, and Shamma, and Shilshah, and Ithran, and Beera” (1 Chronicles 7:37). The next verse names the sons of Jether, which may be another form of the same name. The name means abundance or excellence. One Ithran belonged to a people God removed; the other to a people God kept.

pos: n. (proper name; an Asherite, head of a house)
biblical_def: Ulla is the last-named head of a house in the genealogy of Asher. “And the sons of Ulla; Arah, and Haniel, and Rezia” (1 Chronicles 7:39). The next verse closes the tribe's register: “All these were the children of Asher, heads of their father's house, choice and mighty men of valour, chief of the princes. And the number throughout the genealogy of them that were apt to the war and to battle was twenty and six thousand men” (1 Chronicles 7:40). Ulla's name may mean yoke. Moses' blessing on Asher promised strength for the burden of every day: “Thy shoes shall be iron and brass; and as thy days, so shall thy strength be” (Deuteronomy 33:25). Asher's house of Ulla is named and then the tribe's record ends. Christ invites all who labour to take His yoke, which is easy, and His burden, which is light.

pos: n. (proper name; a Benjamite, son of Bela)
etymology: Hebrew 'Iri, my city or watchful, from 'ir, city, or 'ur, to awake; called Ir in 1 Chronicles 7:12.
biblical_def: Iri is a Benjamite, the fifth son of Bela. “The sons of Benjamin; Bela, and Becher, and Jediael, three” (1 Chronicles 7:6). “And the sons of Bela; Ezbon, and Uzzi, and Uzziel, and Jerimoth, and Iri, five; heads of the house of their fathers, mighty men of valour; and were reckoned by their genealogies twenty and two thousand and thirty and four” (1 Chronicles 7:7). A few verses later the Chronicler names “the children of Ir” (1 Chronicles 7:12), with the margin noting Iri, so the families of Shuppim and Huppim descend from him. Benjamin was the smallest tribe and nearly destroyed in the days of the judges, yet its genealogy records mighty men of valour by the thousand. From Benjamin came Saul the first king and Saul of Tarsus, the apostle. Iri's name may mean watchful; his line was among the heads of a tribe God preserved through near extinction.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God preserves and uses the least, as He kept Benjamin when it was nearly cut off.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'Iri, watchful or my city; a Benjamite, son of Bela.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'Iri, perhaps watchful.
Son of Bela (1 Chronicles 7:7).
Called Ir in 1 Chronicles 7:12.
Head of a house of his fathers.
Father of the houses of Shuppim and Huppim.
usage: Jerimoth, and Iri, five
mighty men of valour
